cards.s: Data & model gates
cards.html:
Chapter 6 · Level 4: ML-Specific CI/CD. Levels 1–3 would work for any web service. This level adds what makes ML delivery different: data contracts, training inside CI, a gate that blocks worse models, a model registry, and an evaluation gate for an LLM-based RAG service, with costs under control.

After this level you can:

  • Validate training data with a pandera contract before training.
  • Train in CI and fail the build when metrics drop (accuracy gate).
  • Track runs in MLflow and promote models with registry aliases.
  • Evaluate a RAG service with a golden set: hit rate, MRR and LLM-judged faithfulness, as a gate.
  • Control LLM costs in CI; schedule nightly evals and weekly retraining.
  • Explain the whole pipeline in an interview in two minutes.

cards.s: Data & model gates
cards.html: What you build: credit-api with data contract, accuracy gate and MLflow champion/challenger promotion; rag-api with a retrieval and faithfulness gate that runs cheaply on PRs and fully every night.

cards.s: Part A · Classic ML: data contract
cards.html:
Most ML incidents start with data: an upstream system changes a unit, a column is renamed, a category appears that never existed. A data contract states what valid training data looks like, and the pipeline checks it before training, so it fails on bad data with a clear message instead of producing a silently bad model.

src/credit_api/validation.py:

cards.s: Part A · Classic ML: data contract
cards.html:
"""Data contract for the training data, written with pandera."""

import pandas as pd
import pandera.pandas as pa

SCHEMA = pa.DataFrameSchema(
    {
        "duration": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.in_range(1, 120)),
        "credit_amount": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.gt(0)),
        "age": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.in_range(18, 100)),
        "checking_status": pa.Column(str, nullable=False),
        "credit_history": pa.Column(str, nullable=False),
        "purpose": pa.Column(str, nullable=False),
        "savings_status": pa.Column(str, nullable=False),
        "employment": pa.Column(str, nullable=False),
        "target": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.isin([0, 1])),
    },
    checks=[
        # at least 15 % of rows must be "bad" so the model can learn it
        pa.Check(
            lambda df: df["target"].mean() >= 0.15,
            error="label share of class 1 below 15 %",
        ),
    ],
    strict=True,
)

def validate(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Raise pandera.errors.SchemaErrors listing every problem found."""
    return SCHEMA.validate(df, lazy=True)

cards.s: Part A · Classic ML: data contract
cards.html:
pandera checks types, ranges and allowed values per column (lines 8–16), and whole-table rules such as a minimum share of the minority class (lines 18–24). strict=True rejects unexpected extra columns. lazy=True (line 31) collects all problems instead of stopping at the first, so one CI run shows everything that is wrong. The tests in test_data.py prove that the contract rejects bad values: a contract that never fails is useless.

What if… the upstream system sends a category we have never seen?

cards.s: Part A · Classic ML: data contract
cards.html:
What happens: A new product launches, and purpose now contains "crypto". Our contract only says purpose is a non-empty string, so validation passes. Training works. At serving time, the OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") turns "crypto" into all zeros: the model predicts as if the purpose were unknown, without any error (the test test_unknown_category_does_not_crash proves it does not crash, which is not the same as "behaves well").

Why: There is a deliberate trade-off. A strict contract (pa.Check.isin([...]) with the known values) stops training on the first new category, which is safe but blocks the weekly retraining for something harmless. A loose one never blocks, and silently degrades.

cards.s: Part A · Classic ML: data contract
cards.html: What you do: Be strict where an unknown value is dangerous and loose where it is merely new, and make "new" visible: log the share of unknown categories at serving time and in the nightly validation, and alert above a few percent. A good middle ground in pandera is a check with a tolerance: "at most 1 % of rows outside the known values".

cards.s: Contracts check **validity**, not **drift**
cards.html:
A contract answers "is every value plausible?". It cannot answer "is this data like the data the model learned from?". We tested this: multiplying every credit_amount by 1.3 (30 % inflation) produces data that passes the contract completely. A two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test compares two distributions and notices at once. Real output, comparing two halves of the data set, then one half against the inflated other half:

drift check (results from a real run):

from scipy.stats import ks_2samp

ks_2samp(ref.credit_amount, new.credit_amount)
# statistic=0.042  pvalue=0.77        same source: no evidence of drift
ks_2samp(ref.credit_amount, inflated.credit_amount)
# statistic=0.184  pvalue=8.2e-08     clear drift

cards.s: Contracts check **validity**, not **drift**
cards.html: In CI, such a check compares the newest training data with a stored reference sample, typically in the nightly data-validation job. Two warnings from practice. With large samples, a p-value flags even tiny, irrelevant differences, so teams threshold the statistic (e.g. KS > 0.1) or use the Population Stability Index (PSI; rule of thumb: < 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 watch, > 0.25 act). And drift is a reason to look, not automatically a reason to fail: inflation is real, and the model may need retraining, not the data rejecting. Libraries such as Evidently produce these reports for every column.

cards.s: Training in CI and the accuracy gate
cards.html:
train() validates, splits with a fixed seed, fits and measures:

src/credit_api/train.py:

def train(
    sample_frac: float = 1.0, max_iter: int = 200
) -> tuple[Pipeline, dict[str, float]]:
    df = validate(sample(load_data(), sample_frac))
    x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        df[FEATURES],
        df[TARGET],
        test_size=0.25,
        stratify=df[TARGET],
        random_state=SEED,
    )
    model = build_pipeline(max_iter=max_iter)
    model.fit(x_train, y_train)
    proba = model.predict_proba(x_test)[:, 1]
    pred = (proba >= 0.5).astype(int)
    metrics = {
        "roc_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba)), 4),
        "accuracy": round(float(accuracy_score(y_test, pred)), 4),
        "f1": round(float(f1_score(y_test, pred)), 4),
        "n_train": float(len(x_train)),
    }
    return model, metrics

cards.s: Training in CI and the accuracy gate
cards.html: With 1,000 rows this takes about a second, so CI can train on the full data. With real data sets you would train on a stratified sample in PR pipelines (--sample-frac 0.1) and on everything only on main or nightly. The point is not to produce the production model in every PR; it is to prove that the pipeline still produces a good model.

cards.s: Training in CI and the accuracy gate
cards.html:
The gate compares the new metrics with two kinds of limits (Figure 15):

  • Floors: absolute minimums (roc_auc ≥ 0.70, f1 ≥ 0.40). Below them, the model is not fit for purpose, whatever the baseline says.
  • Maximum drop: compared with the baseline (the metrics of the model in production, committed as metrics/baseline.json), no metric may fall by more than 0.03. This catches regressions that are still above the floor.

src/credit_api/gate.py:

cards.s: Training in CI and the accuracy gate
cards.html:
def check(
    new: dict[str, float],
    baseline: dict[str, float],
    floors: dict[str, float],
    max_drop: float,
) -> list[str]:
    """Return a list of human-readable failures (empty = pass)."""
    failures = []
    for name, floor in floors.items():
        if new[name] < floor:
            failures.append(f"{name}={new[name]:.4f} below floor {floor}")
        drop = baseline.get(name, 0.0) - new[name]
        if drop > max_drop:
            failures.append(
                f"{name} dropped {drop:.4f} vs baseline (allowed {max_drop})"
            )
    return failures

cards.s: Training in CI and the accuracy gate
cards.html:
In CI the gate is a job of its own (model-gate in ci.yml), which also writes the metrics into the job summary ($GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY), so reviewers see them on the run page without opening logs:

terminal:

cards.s: Training in CI and the accuracy gate
cards.html:
uv run python -m credit_api.train
uv run python -m credit_api.gate metrics/metrics.json

expected output:

roc_auc    new=0.7865 baseline=0.7865
f1         new=0.5231 baseline=0.5231
QUALITY GATE PASSED

Watch out: Gates on noisy metrics

cards.s: Training in CI and the accuracy gate
cards.html: Metrics on small test sets fluctuate. A tolerance that is too tight makes the gate flaky (red without a real problem), and people learn to ignore red builds. Fix the seed, use a large enough test set, choose the tolerance from the run-to-run variance you observe, and update the baseline deliberately, through a PR that changes baseline.json, when a better model ships.

cards.s: Worked example: choosing the tolerance from data
cards.html:
Is max_drop = 0.03 a good value? Do not guess: measure how much the metric moves when nothing meaningful changes. We trained the credit-api model 20 times while varying one source of randomness at a time (uv run python scripts/variance.py; real output):

What variedROC-AUC over 20 runs
Model seed only (same split)0.7865 every time, std 0.0000
Train/test split seedmean 0.7814, std 0.025, min 0.741, max 0.832
Bootstrap of the fixed test set (1,000 resamples)95 % interval 0.728 – 0.851

cards.s: Worked example: choosing the tolerance from data
cards.html:
Three lessons, each with consequences for the gate:

  1. This model has no training randomness. Gradient boosting without subsampling is deterministic here (early stopping, which would add randomness, only switches on automatically above 10,000 rows). So on an unchanged split, any metric change is caused by the code or the data. The 0.03 tolerance is generous for code changes.
  2. The split is worth ±0.05. A PR that "only" changes test_size, the seed, or the order of rows in the CSV moves AUC by as much as a real model regression, in either direction. Rule: the evaluation split is part of the contract. Change it only in a PR that also updates the baseline, and say so.

cards.s: Worked example: choosing the tolerance from data
cards.html:
1. 250 test rows give an uncertainty of ±0.06. Our baseline 0.7865 is one draw from a wide interval. You cannot claim "the new model is better" from a 0.005 improvement on this test set. With real data, use a larger test set; the interval shrinks roughly with 1/√n (four times the rows, half the width).

What if… the gate fails, but I am sure the model is not worse?

What happens: A refactoring PR fails with roc_auc dropped 0.0410 vs baseline (allowed 0.03), although you did not touch the model.

cards.s: Worked example: choosing the tolerance from data
cards.html:
Why: Look for something that changed what is evaluated: the split (seed, test_size, row order after a data cleanup), the set of rows (a filter that now drops duplicates), the features (a column now parsed differently). Lesson 2 above says these alone can move AUC by 0.05.

What you do: Find which. Run the old and the new code on the same rows and compare predictions row by row (np.abs(p_old - p_new).max()): if predictions are identical, the evaluation changed, not the model. Fix the accidental change, or, if it was intentional, update baseline.json in the same PR with an explanation. Do not raise max_drop to make the build green.

cards.s: Gating on slices, not only the average
cards.html:
The overall AUC hides a gap we measured on the test set:

SliceRowsROC-AUC
age ≥ 252020.796
age < 25480.736

cards.s: Gating on slices, not only the average
cards.html:
Young applicants get noticeably worse predictions. A change that improves the average while making this gap worse would pass our gate. A slice gate adds per-segment floors (for example "AUC for age < 25 ≥ 0.70" and "gap ≤ 0.08"), computed in train.py and checked by the same check() function. Be careful with small slices: with 48 rows, the slice AUC itself is very noisy, so set slice floors loosely, or require a minimum slice size before the check applies. In a credit model, which slices to watch is not only a technical choice: anti- discrimination law and the EU AI Act make it a legal one, and the slices belong in the model card.

What if… we decide to accept a slightly worse model on purpose?

cards.s: Gating on slices, not only the average
cards.html:
What happens: Removing the feature age makes the model fairer and simpler to defend, but AUC drops by 0.035. The gate blocks it.

What you do: That is the gate working: it forces the trade-off to be a visible decision. Change metrics/baseline.json in the same PR, explain the trade-off in the PR description, and get an explicit approval (CODEOWNERS can make a specific person's review mandatory for changes to metrics/). The Git history then records who accepted which metric change, and why: exactly what an auditor will ask for.
